exercises.prompt: Implement unique(xs) so it returns a set of the distinct values in xs, with duplicates collapsed. unique([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]) is {1, 2, 3}. An empty list returns an empty set, written set() (not {}, which is an empty dict).
hints: A set stores each value at most once, so it dedupes for free — the task is just getting your list's values into one.
The set() constructor takes any list and keeps only the distinct values: set([1, 1, 2]) is {1, 2}.
return set(xs) — returning a list would fail, since a set is compared by membership not order, and the empty case must be set(), because {} is an empty dict.

exercises.prompt: Implement union(a, b), where a and b are lists, so it returns a set of every value that appears in either list, with duplicates collapsed. union([1, 2], [2, 3]) is {1, 2, 3}. Two empty lists return an empty set, set().
exercises.solution:
def union(a, b):
    return set(a) | set(b)
hints: A set already removes duplicates, so if you pour both lists into sets and combine them, the overlap collapses on its own.
The | operator unions two sets: set(a) | set(b) keeps every value from either side, once each.
return set(a) | set(b) — the size test proves the value shared by both lists is counted only once.

exercises.prompt: Implement intersection(a, b), where a and b are lists, so it returns a set of the values that appear in BOTH lists, with duplicates collapsed. intersection([1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4]) is {2, 3}. If the lists share nothing, or either is empty, the result is an empty set, set().
exercises.solution:
def intersection(a, b):
    return set(a) & set(b)
hints: You want the values common to both — a set keeps each once, which is exactly the shape of the answer.
The & operator intersects two sets: set(a) & set(b) keeps only values present on both sides.
return set(a) & set(b) — the duplicate-heavy test proves repeats collapse to a single value in the result.

exercises.prompt: Implement difference(a, b), where a and b are lists, so it returns a set of the values that appear in a but NOT in b, with duplicates collapsed. difference([1, 2, 3], [2]) is {1, 3}. If every value of a is also in b, or a is empty, the result is an empty set, set().
exercises.solution:
def difference(a, b):
    return set(a) - set(b)
hints: This is the intersection idea with the test flipped: keep the values of a that are not in b.
The - operator subtracts one set from another: set(a) - set(b) drops every value that b contains.
return set(a) - set(b) — the membership test confirms a value present in b is absent from the result.

exercises.prompt: Implement has_duplicates(xs) so it returns True when some value appears more than once in xs, and False when every value is distinct. has_duplicates([1, 2, 2]) is True; has_duplicates([1, 2, 3]) is False. An empty list has no duplicates, so it returns False. Return a bool.
hints: Building a set drops duplicates, so if the set is smaller than the list, something must have collapsed.
Compare the two sizes: len(set(xs)) is the count of distinct values, len(xs) the total.
return len(set(xs)) != len(xs) — equal sizes mean no repeats (False), including the empty list; the non-adjacent test proves repeats are caught anywhere.
